level.name: Augmented
level.tagline: AI is part of the standard workflow
level.description: AI is part of the team's standard workflow. Shared agent guidance exists and guardrails are solid (real test suite, CI gates, enforced types/lint), so AI-generated code is safe to merge.

posture.label: Solid but Manual
posture.blurb: Strong engineering foundations with untapped AI leverage — operationalize AI tooling.

signals: 1/30 commits carry an AI co-author trailer

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions
dimensions.summary: No machine-readable agent guidance was found anywhere in the sampled content — no CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, copilot-instructions.md, or MCP config, and nothing in the README or workflow files references AI tooling conventions. For a 32k-star, high-traffic OSS library, this is a near-total absence of AI-native contributor tooling, matching the signal's 0 baseline with only marginal credit for the existence of a CONTRIBUTING.md that could eventually anchor such guidance.
evidence: No machine-readable AI/agent guidance detected (e.g. CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules)
strengths: CONTRIBUTING.md exists as a potential foundation to extend with agent-facing instructions
CI workflows already codify canonical commands (pnpm run-all-checks, pnpm test-typing, pnpm test:e2e) that a future CLAUDE.md could simply surface
gaps: No CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md documenting build/test/run commands or architecture
No .cursorrules, copilot-instructions.md, or equivalent tool-specific config
No MCP server configuration or prompt/skill library
No explicit 'never/always' constraints or subpackage architecture map (core vs. infinite/immutable/mutation/subscription) for agents to follow

dimensions.name: Automated Testing
dimensions.summary: Testing is this repository's strongest dimension: 138 test files against a 1.04 test-to-source ratio, a configured test framework, Playwright-driven e2e tests covering dev/prod build modes and React version matrices (legacy 17, stable, canary), and coverage tracking. Sampled e2e specs show genuine behavioral and regression coverage (concurrent-transition/isPending semantics, suspense retry paths, RSC cache prefill, a named regression test tied to issue #2702) rather than superficial smoke tests.
strengths: 138 test files with a 1.04 test-to-source ratio — unusually high rigor
Playwright e2e suite exercising dev and prod build modes plus React 17/stable/canary matrices
Tests target specific behavioral edge cases and past regressions (e.g. issue-2702, concurrent transitions, suspense retry)
Coverage tracking configured alongside a dedicated test-typing check
gaps: No mutation testing (Stryker-equivalent) evidenced
No accessibility testing (axe/pa11y) evidenced, though less critical for a headless data-fetching library
No explicit coverage-threshold gate confirmed in the sampled CI config

dimensions.name: CI/CD & Delivery
dimensions.summary: CI is broad and disciplined: 5 workflows run lint, full test suite, type-checking, package-export validation (attw), and a matrixed e2e suite across dev/prod modes inside a Playwright container, plus dedicated scheduled canary-React testing. A separate release workflow implements npm OIDC trusted publishing with prerelease-tag detection (beta/canary/rc), and the commit history's bare version-bump commits point to an automated release-versioning flow layered on top — slightly ahead of what the raw signal bullets alone credit.
strengths: 5 workflows covering lint/test/build/e2e/type-checking, including a nightly React-canary compatibility run
E2E matrix runs both dev and prod build modes in a containerized Playwright environment
Dedicated release workflow using npm OIDC trusted publishing with automatic prerelease-tag routing
Branch protection requiring PRs, approvals, and code-owner review gates the same pipeline
gaps: No IaC/GitOps/progressive-delivery evidence (likely not applicable to a client-side library)
Action references in workflows are not pinned to SHAs, weakening the pipeline's supply-chain integrity
Release trigger is manual (workflow_dispatch) rather than fully tag-driven automation
No explicit coverage-threshold merge gate confirmed

dimensions.name: Agentic Workflows
dimensions.summary: No agentic workflows were detected: no AI code-review bot (CodeRabbit, Claude/Copilot review actions), no LLM invocation inside CI, no auto-fix/auto-format bot, and no Dependabot/Renovate auto-merge configuration in the sampled files. The CI pipeline is thorough but entirely human-driven from PR to merge, with process signals showing only 0.5 average reviews per PR — no autonomous review or fix loop compounds that.
evidence: No agentic/AI-in-CI workflows detected (e.g. AI review bots, LLM steps in CI, auto-merge)
gaps: No AI review bot wired into pull requests
No LLM step embedded in any CI workflow
No auto-fix/auto-PR tooling
No dependency-update bot (Dependabot/Renovate) with auto-merge detected

dimensions.name: Documentation & Knowledge
dimensions.summary: Documentation is solid for human contributors — a substantial, feature-rich README, a CONTRIBUTING.md, and a working examples/ directory with runnable sample apps (the api-hooks example shows a full fetch/hook/page pattern) — but there's no dedicated docs/ or ADR directory, no CHANGELOG.md despite frequent versioned releases, and nothing oriented specifically toward agent consumption.
strengths: Substantial README (3737 chars) covering features, quick start, and links to full docs site
CONTRIBUTING.md present, indicating a defined contribution path
Working examples/ directory with a complete runnable sample app (hooks, fetcher, pages)
gaps: No CHANGELOG.md detected despite an active versioned release cadence (2.5.0, betas)
No ADR or docs/decisions directory evidenced
No generated API reference (typedoc) referenced in the sample
Documentation appears human-oriented only, with no agent-readable architecture map

dimensions.name: Code Quality & Guardrails
dimensions.summary: Guardrails are well enforced: TypeScript strict mode plus additional strictness flags (noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters, noFallthroughCasesInSwitch), a formatter/linter recently migrated to oxfmt/oxlint, pre-commit hooks, a CODEOWNERS file naming two maintainers, and branch protection requiring 1 approval plus code-owner review and signed commits. The one soft spot is that only 56% of sampled merged PRs actually carry an approving review despite the required-approval rule, suggesting a bypass path (e.g. maintainer self-merge) coexists with the formal gate.
evidence: PR review coverage 56% (18 merged · 70% small · 0% reverted)
Pull requests required to merge (1 approval(s) + code owners)
strengths: TypeScript strict mode with several additional strictness compiler flags enabled
Formatter/linter actively maintained (recent migration from ESLint to oxlint/oxfmt)
CODEOWNERS plus branch protection requiring approval, code-owner review, and signed commits
Pre-commit hooks configured
gaps: Only 56% of merged PRs show an approving review despite the required-approval rule — a possible bypass path
No PR template evidenced in the signals
Conventional-commit style (67%) is not enforced via commitlint, only informally adopted

dimensions.name: Commit & Velocity Signals
dimensions.summary: Commit signals show an actively maintained project with disciplined batching (70% small PRs), 67% conventional-commit adoption, and very fast merge velocity (0.6h median time-to-merge) — but AI involvement in the commit history is minimal, with only 1 of 30 recent commits showing AI co-authorship, and a notable gap between fast merges (0.6h) and slower first review (17.6h) worth understanding.
strengths: Active cadence, pushed within the last 30 days
67% conventional-commit prefix adoption
70% small-PR rate indicating disciplined batch size
Fast median time-to-merge (0.6h)
gaps: Only 1 of 30 recent commits shows AI co-authorship — negligible AI footprint in history
Time-to-first-review (17.6h) is far slower than time-to-merge (0.6h), an unusual gap worth investigating
Conventional-commit adoption is partial (67%), not fully consistent

dimensions.name: AI Process & Harness
dimensions.summary: Process discipline exists at the human-contribution level — structured issue templates and a heavily protected default branch (7 ruleset rules including signed commits) — but there is no structured harness for verifying AI-produced changes specifically: no evals/golden-test directory, no prompt or agent-spec library, and no agent-readable runbooks or Definition-of-Done for AI-assisted contributions.
strengths: Structured issue templates in place
Default branch protected with 7 ruleset rules including signed-commit enforcement
gaps: No evals or golden-test directory for AI/LLM output
No structured prompt/agent library (prompts/, .claude/agents/)
No agent-readable operational runbooks or ADRs
No Definition-of-Done or CONTRIBUTING guidance specific to AI-assisted changes

dimensions.name: Supply Chain & Security
dimensions.summary: Security posture scores 40/100 on the deterministic battery: branch protection and dangerous-workflow patterns are strong (8/10 and 10/10) and a SECURITY.md policy is present (10/10), but supply-chain automation is largely missing — no SAST wired into CI, no committed dependency-update tool, 0 of 8 Action references pinned by SHA, no artifact signing/provenance step recognized, and no SBOM generation. Exposure (actual known vulnerabilities) could not be assessed since no lockfile or advisory access was available. Given the package's scale (32k stars, broad downstream usage), the gap between strong access-control posture and weak build-pipeline hardening is the more consequential half of this score.
evidence: Branch protection [posture/high]: 8/10 — Default branch: protected, 1 approval(s), code-owner review, signed commits.
Dangerous workflow [posture/critical]: 10/10 — No script-injection or untrusted-checkout patterns detected.
Token permissions [posture/high]: 2/10 — 1/5 workflows set an explicit `permissions:` scope; 1 grant broad write.
SAST [posture/medium]: 0/10 — No SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep/Sonar) wired into CI.
Dependency updates [posture/high]: 0/10 — No dependency-update tool committed.
Pinned dependencies [posture/medium]: 0/10 — 0/8 Actions/images pinned by SHA/digest (8 action refs).
Security policy [posture/medium]: 10/10 — SECURITY.md documents a vulnerability-reporting path.
Signed releases [posture/high]: 0/10 — No artifact signing / provenance in CI.
Known vulnerabilities [exposure/high]: n/a/10 — Dependency vulnerabilities not inspected (no lockfile / no alert access).
strengths: Branch protection enforces 1 approval, code-owner review, and signed commits
No dangerous workflow patterns (script injection, untrusted checkout) detected
SECURITY.md documents a vulnerability-reporting path
Release workflow implements npm OIDC trusted publishing, a provenance-adjacent mechanism not credited by the raw signed-releases check
gaps: Add CodeQL (or Semgrep) scanning that runs on pull_request.
Add a `.github/dependabot.yml` (or Renovate) config.
Pin third-party Actions to a full commit SHA (and container images to a digest).
Sign releases with cosign and emit SLSA provenance (actions/attest).
Generate an SBOM (Syft/CycloneDX) on release.
Add a least-privilege top-level `permissions:` block (default `contents: read`) to every workflow.

headline: SWR is a textbook example of disciplined traditional OSS engineering — deep test coverage, gated CI, and enforced branch protection — but shows almost no AI-native tooling or agentic automation, landing it at the low end of L3 (Augmented) overall.
strengths: Exceptional automated test coverage: 138 test files, a 1.04 test-to-source ratio, and a Playwright e2e suite exercising dev/prod builds across React version matrices
CI pipeline gates every merge with lint, type-check, build, and e2e across 5 workflows, including nightly React-canary compatibility testing
Strong code-quality guardrails: TypeScript strict mode, an actively maintained linter/formatter, CODEOWNERS, and branch protection requiring approval, code-owner review, and signed commits
Mature release engineering, including npm OIDC trusted publishing and clear prerelease channels (beta/canary)
Active, fast-moving maintenance cadence with small, frequent PRs and largely conventional commit messages
risks: No machine-readable AI agent guidance exists anywhere in the repo (no CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), so any AI contribution today is necessarily ad hoc rather than convention-driven
Zero agentic workflows are wired in — no AI review bot, no LLM-in-CI step, no auto-fix or dependency auto-merge — so nothing autonomous currently compounds the strong human-driven CI
Supply-chain automation lags the project's exposure: no SAST, no dependency-update bot, and 0 of 8 Action references pinned by SHA, despite the package's broad downstream reach
56% of sampled merged PRs lack a recorded approving review despite a required-approval branch-protection rule, suggesting a bypass path (e.g. maintainer self-merge)
AI involvement in commit history is negligible (1 of 30 recent commits), so there's little behavioral evidence yet of an AI-native contribution pattern to build guardrails around

roadmap.title: Agents have no shared playbook — there's no CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md for contributors or coding agents to follow
roadmap.rationale: Without a machine-readable guidance file, any AI agent (or new human contributor) touching this codebase has to rediscover build/test/lint commands and the subpackage architecture (core hooks vs. infinite/immutable/mutation/subscription, react-server exports) from scratch — that tacit knowledge is exactly what a shared doc would carry, and its absence is likely the single largest gap holding the repo back from the next trust tier.
explore: What would an agent need to know before it could safely touch core cache/revalidation logic without a maintainer walking it through first?
Is there tacit knowledge (e.g. the react-server/RSC export split, the multi-target bunchee build) that currently only lives in maintainers' heads?
Would surfacing the commands already used in CI (pnpm run-all-checks, pnpm test-typing, pnpm test:e2e) into a lightweight CLAUDE.md be enough to start?

roadmap.title: No agentic loop touches review or delivery — CI checks code, but nothing autonomous reviews, fixes, or ships it
roadmap.rationale: The pipeline gates well (lint/test/build/e2e all run), but every step from PR feedback to merge still depends entirely on human review — averaging 0.5 reviews per PR with 56% reviewed coverage — and there's no AI review bot, dependency auto-merge, or LLM-in-CI step compounding that effort. Even one agentic touchpoint would be a visible step toward L4-style autonomy.
explore: Where in the current review cycle (17.6h median time-to-first-review) would an AI review pass add the most leverage without slowing anything down?

Is the team open to a bot handling low-risk, mechanical PRs (dependency bumps, docs) end-to-end, or does the library's reach (32k stars, broad downstream usage) argue for keeping humans in that loop longer?
Would advisory AI review comments (rather than a merge gate) be a lower-risk way to build trust in the loop first?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain automation hasn't caught up to the project's exposure — no SAST, no dependency-update bot, and unpinned Action references
roadmap.rationale: This is a widely-depended-on package, which raises the stakes of a compromised CI Action or an unpatched transitive dependency well above a typical repo's; right now 0 of 8 Action references are pinned to a SHA, there's no committed Dependabot/Renovate config, and no SAST tool runs in CI, so automated guardrails haven't grown to match the project's blast radius.
explore: Given the download volume, would pinning the 8 GitHub Action references to SHAs be a quick, low-risk first move?
Is dependency-update automation (Dependabot/Renovate) something the team has consciously deferred, or just hasn't gotten to yet?
Would a lightweight SAST pass (e.g. CodeQL, free for public repos) fit naturally into the existing test.yml workflow?

roadmap.title: There's no structured harness for verifying AI-authored changes — no evals, prompt library, or agent-specific contribution guidance
roadmap.rationale: Issue templates and heavy branch protection show a disciplined human contribution process, but nothing yet would let AI-generated changes be verified systematically (evals/golden tests) or produced consistently (a prompts/ or agents/ library) — as AI-assisted contributions grow, this is the piece that turns one-off prompting into a repeatable, trustworthy pipeline.
explore: If an agent proposed a change to SWR's revalidation logic today, what would give the team confidence to merge it without a full manual re-review?
Would documenting a Definition-of-Done for AI-assisted PRs be useful now, or is it premature given how few AI-authored commits exist so far (1 of 30)?
Is there appetite for a small evals/ suite if AI-assisted contributions increase over time?

roadmap.title: Branch protection requires review, yet under half of recent merges show an approving review on record
roadmap.rationale: The ruleset requires 1 approval plus code-owner review, but only 56% of sampled merged PRs carry an approving review — that gap (likely maintainer self-merges or an admin bypass) is worth understanding before layering more AI-authored changes on top, since it's the exact guardrail that would need to hold consistently as AI contributions increase.
explore: Do the unreviewed merges represent maintainer-authored, low-risk changes, or is there a bypass path worth revisiting?
Would tightening that gap now make it easier to extend the same trusted path to AI-authored PRs later?

discrepancies.claim: The 'Signed releases' check reports 0/10 with no provenance detected, but trigger-release.yml explicitly sets permissions: id-token: write and installs npm >=11.5.1 specifically to enable OIDC trusted publishing, which generates Sigstore-backed provenance attestations for npm packages — a form of signed-release provenance the check appears not to have credited.

The recent commit history contains bare version-bump commits ('2.5.0 (#4309)', '2.5.0-beta.1 (#4299)', '2.5.0-beta.0 (#4291)') alongside a dedicated OIDC publish workflow, evidence of an automated release-versioning flow that the D3 signal list (which only cites test/lint/build) doesn't appear to credit.

blockers: No agent memory (.ai/memory) — decisions and gotchas aren't carried between sessions.
No reusable agent skills library (.claude/skills) — repeated work is re-prompted each time.
Agent can't self-verify: missing typecheck script(s).
Zero observability: no error tracking, structured logs, metrics, or tracing.
CI does not gate merges (no enforced required checks).
